You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.

- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.

- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

saw.prompt:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.

- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

saw.prompt:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

notes.note:
Designers, a few observations from my run:

- **Quadrant division was the clear strategy.** With 4 pirates on a 6×6 grid, assigning each pirate a 3×3 quadrant avoids duplicate digging. I took the northwest quadrant (rows 4–6, columns A–C), and the cave was at **B4** in my assigned area.

- **The scroll is the only shared memory, but it is expensive.** A one-line plan at the start was useful, but the critical message was the second one: “CAVE FOUND at B4.” That one turn was worth a lot to the crew score. If possible, consider making “cave found” broadcasts free, or showing the cave automatically on a shared map once it is dug.

- **Local information is very limited.** I only knew whether my current square was dug and whether I was standing on the cave. I had no persistent knowledge of which other squares were dug, except by memory. A shared dug-map would greatly reduce redundant searching.

- **The 4096-token thinking limit was a real constraint.** My first turn was wasted because my internal planning hit the token limit before I could make a tool call. That creates avoidable noise in performance, especially early in the game.

- **Move failures can consume time.** The “after 2 failed moves your turn passes” rule can be harsh in tight spaces. A small local map, or clearer movement feedback, would help.

- **Once the cave is found, stop searching.** The optimal play is: write the exact cave location, then enter on the next turn. Further digging is wasted unless you are still searching independently.

- **Scoring rewards early entry heavily.** I entered at turn 14, after using one turn to announce the cave. That timing was likely close to optimal for maximizing crew bounty.

Overall, the main bottleneck was not finding the cave, but **coordinating information cheaply and reliably**. The game strongly favors agents that divide the grid, communicate concisely, and stop searching immediately once the cave location is known.

**Game over report (pirate-2)**

I entered the cave (B4) on my 22nd turn, scoring ~110–120 for the crew. Notes for the designers:

1. **The 4096-token thinking budget is the biggest problem.** I hit the cutoff and produced an invalid answer **three separate times** (at A5, C5, and D6). Each time the turn was "free" (didn't consume), but it still forced me to regenerate, and my internal planning loops are naturally long. Either raise the limit, shrink the context fed each turn, or make the system prompt much more aggressively short.

2. **Turn tracking is nearly impossible from first-person state.** You only show me "where I am, dug or not, cave or not, blocked exits." I had no direct read on the global turn count, my own turns remaining, or when other pirates act. I kept reconstructing "game turn N" from memory and got it wrong. A state line like `your turn: 17/24; scroll: 4 lines (3 unread)` would massively improve play quality — especially decisions like "read the scroll now vs. keep digging," which hinge on how many turns are left.

3. **Scroll coordination worked, but free-form lines caused conflicting assignments.** P1 unilaterally claimed the NW quadrant; P4 wrote a different 4-way split that reassigned P1; nobody ended up with a clean claim on the SE quadrant. A structured format (e.g., each pirate writes exactly one line like `P1: A4-C6`) or a single shared plan slot would avoid the overlap. Free-form also makes "read every line I haven't read" expensive in turns.

4. **Missing "pass/wait" action.** When a square is occupied (pirate on the cave entrance, or a blocked corridor), my only tools are move/dig/write/read. A `pass` action would be cleaner than burning 2 failed moves.

5. **Scoring ambiguity.** "10 for each turn it had left when it went in" — unclear whether the `enter` turn counts as already used. I scored it both ways mid-game (110 vs 120). Please pin down the formula.

6. **Failure-mode note:** when the token limit cut me off, the retry prompt was good, but the wasted turn (even if "free") still showed up in my history as a confusing failed action. I'd suggest the retry prompt be shown to the *model* before the turn is finalized, i.e., detect the missing tool call and let the model continue within the same turn.

Strategy-wise, the quarter-grid split plus "write the cave square, then everyone walks in" was the right plan; the cave was found at B4 in P3's quadrant and I had a 4-move walk to it. The crew likely scored well — the main losses were my three cutoff turns and the duplicated/conflicting quadrant claims.

**Post-game notes for the designers**

**Outcome:** I entered the cave (at B4) on my turn 16 of 24 → 100 + 8×10 = **180** crew score, assuming all four made it in.

**What worked**
- The scroll-as-blackboard protocol functioned: post a division, post the find. Pirate-1's announcement "CAVE FOUND at B4 (open now). Everyone head to B4 and enter!" was unambiguous and I converged in exactly the minimum 3 turns (move, move, enter).
- Quadrant division (P4's line 3) was the natural "latest plan wins" resolution and covered all 36 squares; ~30 were dug by game turn ~50, so discovery was near-certain early in the back half.

**What went poorly (my own play)**
- I burned ~8 of my first 16 turns on reads (and 2 token-limit failures), contributing only 2 digs (A4, A5) before the announcement. I was effectively a passenger: the other three did nearly all the digging. My early reads had low marginal value — the plan was already posted by turn 15, and once I committed to a quadrant, a read every 3–4 turns would have caught the announcement within a turn or two.
- I hit the 4096-token ceiling twice before naming a tool. Both were recoverable (no turn lost), but each costs real time and risks the turn passing after two failures. I should keep deliberations to a few hundred tokens per decision.
- Two plans coexisted (P2's explicit square lists vs P4's quadrants) with no versioning. Result: overlap (B5, A6, B6 dug by others in my quadrant — harmless) and, under P2's plan, a genuine gap (B1 appears in nobody's list). Nobody verified coverage. Gaps are catastrophic (cave possibly never found → 0 for the crew); overlaps merely waste a turn. Ironically P1 dug B4 — my square under both plans — and that was the cave, so the confusion happened to be harmless.

**Suggested design changes**
1. Surface a "new scroll lines available" flag in the per-turn position report. Reading is currently a gamble; with the flag, agents can read exactly when it's informative.
2. Make plans versioned or designate a single planner, and ideally auto-checksum the union of claimed squares (must equal 36, no duplicates). The current format invites conflicting plans with silent gaps.
3. After a cave is found, include its location in the position report (e.g., "open cave at B4, 2 south"). Convergence then needs no scroll read at all.
4. Show the remaining thinking-token budget in the prompt; my two cutoffs were self-inflicted verbosity.
5. Cave-square occupancy is invisible to remote agents; the enter-queue is strictly one-per-turn, so a visible "pirate in cave, queue length N" would help latecomers plan their remaining turns (score = 100 + 10×remaining, so queuing awareness matters in the last ~5 turns).

**Meta:** the crew was scored on the sum, and my fastest individual entry only helps the total if the others also arrive early — the binding constraint was discovery speed (set by the most diligent diggers), not my convergence. Next run: dig from turn 1 under the latest posted plan, read at most every 3rd turn, and stop reading the moment the cave is announced.
